what_it_does: When a large language model generates text one word at a time, it must at each step consult a growing store of precomputed notes — called a key-value cache — that records context from every previous word. Reading that entire store for every new word wastes memory bandwidth (the speed at which data travels between the chip's memory and its math units). This paper introduces Sella, a chip design that predicts, before reading, which cached notes will actually matter for the current word, and fetches only those. It does this by grouping cached notes into clusters and using a small prediction circuit to score each cluster's likely relevance, so irrelevant entries are skipped entirely. The result is lower memory traffic and faster, more energy-efficient inference on a custom chip (an ASIC — a chip built for exactly one job).
